name: Thales of Miletus - olive presses
instrument: Deposits reserving all olive presses in Miletus & Chios (a call option on press capacity)
entry_exit: Paid small off-season deposits; rented presses out at his own price when a bumper harvest came
ret_risk: Unquantified ('made a lot of money'); premium was small
signals: Forecast of a large harvest (attributed to astronomy); no competing bidders in winter
failure: Poor harvest -> deposits lost (loss capped at premium)
sources: Aristotle, Politics I.11 (1259a), written ~250 years later as a parable

name: Richard Cantillon - Mississippi System
instrument: Mississippi Co. shares, then short the livre / Law's paper via bills of exchange; loans against shares
entry_exit: Bought early, sold into the 1719 surge (shares 500 -> ~10,000 livres), moved into foreign currency, then collected on loans after the crash
ret_risk: 'Two fortunes'; magnitude uncertain (tens of millions of livres claimed)
signals: Law printing unbacked notes to hold shares at 9,000 livres -> currency must fall; insider view of the System
failure: Expelled by Law; years of lawsuits from borrowers; political confiscation risk
sources: Murphy (1986) Richard Cantillon: Entrepreneur and Economist

name: Thomas Guy - sells South Sea stock
entry_exit: Accumulated for ~GBP 42-54k; sold April-June 1720 for GBP 234,428, months before the September crash
signals: Stock up ~8x in 6 months on company-financed purchases and serial subscriptions
failure: Selling early was the only 'risk'; holding on (like Newton) was the real danger
sources: Thomas Guy biographies; Odlyzko (2019) Notes & Records 73(1)

name: Nathan Rothschild - Waterloo myth vs. the consols trade
entry_exit: MYTH: killing on early Waterloo news (traced to an 1846 antisemitic pamphlet). FACT (Ferguson): bought consols after the war, sold in 1817 after a >40% rise
ret_risk: ~+40% on a very large position; ~GBP 600m in today's money (Ferguson)
signals: End of 20+ years of war borrowing -> falling yields; he was initially long gold (wrong side)
failure: Renewed war/inflation; he first lost on bullion when peace cut demand
sources: Ferguson (1998) House of Rothschild; Ferguson (2008) Ascent of Money; Cathcart (2015) The News from Waterloo

name: Cornelius Vanderbilt - Harlem Railroad corners
instrument: Harlem Railroad stock vs. short sellers (incl. NY aldermen)
entry_exit: Controlled the float; shorts forced to cover at ~$179 (1863) and ~$285 (1864) vs. ~$10 in 1862
ret_risk: Order of 10-30x on stock bought early (uncertain)
signals: Shorts > float; opponents' political manipulation
failure: Would be illegal manipulation today (Exchange Act s.9)
sources: Gordon (1988) The Scarlet Woman of Wall Street; Renehan (2007) Commodore

name: Northern Pacific corner
entry_exit: Harriman vs. Hill/Morgan control fight: ~$100-110 -> $1,000 intraday on 9 May 1901; shorts settled at $150
ret_risk: Up to ~10x for holders who sold into the peak
signals: Two buyers competing for a majority + large short interest + delivery deadlines
failure: Shorts ruined; market-wide panic as they dumped other stocks
sources: NYT 10 May 1901; 'Panic of 1901' (Wikipedia summary of contemporary press)

name: Jesse Livermore - Union Pacific short
entry_exit: Shorted days before the San Francisco earthquake
signals: 'Hunch' about an extended market; mostly luck
failure: A rally would have hurt a margined short

name: Jesse Livermore - Panic of 1907
entry_exit: Short into the call-money squeeze; reportedly ~$1m in a day, ~$3m for the episode; covered and went long at J.P. Morgan's urging
signals: Bank runs, call money >100%
failure: Lost it all within a year (cotton, 1908)

name: Jesse Livermore - 1929 crash
entry_exit: Built shorts through 1929 after early losses; reported ~$100m profit
ret_risk: Unknown; figure contested (he denied it at the time)
signals: Extreme margin debt, speculation, weakening breadth
failure: He was early and lost first; bankrupt again by 1934; suicide 1940

name: Joseph P. Kennedy - exits before 1929
entry_exit: Sold most stock before the crash and shorted; profited from pools (legal then)
signals: Speculative excess (the 'shoeshine boy' story first appears in a 1965 biography - folklore)
failure: Pools were outlawed in 1934 - he became the first SEC chairman
sources: Nasaw (2012) The Patriarch; Barry Popik on the shoeshine anecdote

name: Buy the 1932 low (rule-based)
instrument: US stock market (S&P composite, dividends reinvested)
entry_exit: Monthly low Jun 1932 (-86% from 1929 top, CAPE 5.6, dividend yield ~14%)
ret_risk: Real total return: 2.5x in 1y, 4.0x in 5y, 2.5x in 10y, 8.0x in 20y; 1,808x to date (8.3%/yr real)
signals: -86% drawdown, CAPE ~5-6, deflation, bank failures, regime change in policy (1933)
failure: Buying at -80% (Apr 1932) still meant a further -30%; 1937-38 fell 54% again

name: John Templeton - 104 stocks under $1
instrument: $100 of each of 104 NYSE/AMEX stocks priced <= $1 (34 in bankruptcy)
entry_exit: Borrowed $10,000 when WWII began (Sep 1939); sold after ~4 years for ~$40,000; 100 of 104 profitable, 4 worthless
ret_risk: ~4x on the basket (more on his equity, since fully borrowed)
signals: War panic; stocks priced as options on survival; war demand would revive industry
sizing: All-in on borrowed money, but diversified across 104 names
failure: Allied defeat / prolonged depression -> he would owe $10k from salary
sources: Templeton & Phillips (2008) Investing the Templeton Way; Templeton biographies

name: Buy the 1942 low (rule-based)
entry_exit: Monthly low Apr 1942 (-77% below 1929 peak, CAPE 8.5) during Pacific defeats
signals: War news at its worst; CAPE < 10
failure: 1946-49 bear market and post-war inflation cut 5-yr real returns

name: Graham-Newman buys half of GEICO
instrument: Private block: 50% of GEICO from the founding family
entry_exit: Paid $712,500 (~10% below book); stake distributed to fund holders; market value ~$400m at the 1972 peak (reported)
portfolio: ~25% of fund assets; Graham: this one decision out-earned all others combined
signals: Low-cost direct insurer with superior economics, bought below book from a motivated seller
failure: GEICO later fell ~95% (1972-76) and nearly failed
sources: Graham, The Intelligent Investor (postscript); Graham-Newman histories

name: Buffett Partnership - American Express
entry_exit: Salad-oil scandal: $61.8 -> $35.3 (Jun 1964); bought ~$13m at ~$41 avg; sold 1967-68
signals: Liability finite vs. franchise value; merchants & customers still used AmEx cards/cheques
failure: Liability larger than feared / brand damage

name: Li Ka-shing - Hong Kong 1967 riots
entry_exit: Bought from fleeing owners after the 1967 riots; Cheung Kong (1971) built ~1 in 7 private flats in HK by 1983
ret_risk: Unquantified; foundation of a multi-billion fortune
signals: Political panic + emigration while the administrative/legal system held
failure: Chinese takeover/expropriation (the tail that made it cheap)

name: Gold after the Nixon shock
entry_exit: $35 official (Aug 1971) -> $850 London fix (21 Jan 1980)
signals: Bretton Woods strain, falling US gold cover, rising inflation, fixed price below market
failure: Holders at the 1980 top lost ~2/3 in 2 years and waited until 2008 to break even nominally

name: Buffett - Washington Post
entry_exit: $10.6m in the 1973-74 bear (~1/4 of appraised value) -> $221m by 1985
signals: Private-market value ~$400m vs. ~$80m market cap; Watergate-era pressure; 1974 bear
failure: Fell further after purchase; newspapers' later structural decline

name: Buy the 1974 low (rule-based)
entry_exit: Daily low 3 Oct 1974 (-48%, CAPE 8.3)
signals: -48% drawdown, CAPE < 10, oil shock, stagflation
failure: High inflation in 1977-81 held real returns down for a decade

name: Buffett - GEICO rescue
instrument: GEICO common + convertible preferred in the recapitalisation
entry_exit: Stock ~$2 (from ~$61 in 1972); $45.7m invested 1976-80 -> $1.68bn market value at end-1994; 1995-96 buy-out of the rest implied ~$2.3bn for Berkshire's half
signals: Franchise intact; new CEO; recapitalisation under way
failure: Failed recap -> wipe-out

name: Charlie Munger - Belridge Oil
entry_exit: Bought 300 shares at $115; declined 1,500 more; Shell paid $3,665/share (1979)
portfolio: Tiny (~$34.5k) - he called passing on more his biggest error
signals: Market cap far below value of oil reserves; illiquidity kept it cheap
failure: Illiquidity; oil price collapse

name: Carlos Slim - Mexico 1982
entry_exit: Bought during the debt crisis/capital flight (e.g. Reynolds Aluminum & General Tire affiliates, Sanborns, Frisco ~$50m)
signals: Default, devaluation, capital flight, foreign parents dumping subsidiaries
failure: Nationalisation (banks were nationalised in 1982)

name: Buy the 1982 low (rule-based)
entry_exit: Daily low 12 Aug 1982 (-27% from 1980 high; CAPE 6.6, 10y yield ~13%)
signals: CAPE < 8 and Volcker pivot (Fed easing summer 1982)
failure: Low drawdown depth: a drawdown rule alone would not have fired

name: Soros - yen after the Plaza Accord
entry_exit: Positions larger than the fund; ~$150m in a day after the 22 Sep 1985 accord
signals: Overvalued dollar; Baker Treasury shift; G5 meeting
failure: Intervention failure; 1987 shows the same style's crash risk
sources: Soros (1987) The Alchemy of Finance; Time; macro_fx_trades.csv

name: Paul Tudor Jones - 1987 crash
entry_exit: Positioned using a 1929 price analog; covered around the crash
signals: +44% YTD rally with 10y yields 7%->10%, weak dollar, portfolio-insurance feedback, 1929 analog
sizing: Leveraged futures with tight risk control
failure: Analog charts fail far more often than they work
sources: Mallaby (2010) More Money Than God; Tudor Investment Corp. (Wikipedia)

name: Nassim Taleb - 1987 crash
entry_exit: Held a large long-convexity book; Fed liquidity flood made it explode
ret_risk: Reported $35-40m for First Boston; multiple on premium unknown
signals: Cheap wings; belief that markets under-price tails
failure: Premium decay if nothing happens (the usual outcome)

name: Andy Krieger - short NZD
instrument: Leveraged NZD options at Bankers Trust
entry_exit: Shorted the kiwi after the crash; reported ~$300m for the bank
signals: Thin market, high-yield currency after a global risk shock
failure: NZD was HIGHER 6 months later (+3.3%, FRED): tactical, not durable; 'bigger than NZ money supply' is folklore

name: Buffett - Coca-Cola
entry_exit: $1.299bn bought 1988-89 after the crash -> $13.4bn by end-1998
signals: Global brand, buybacks, focus under Goizueta; post-crash valuation
failure: Over-valuation by 1998 -> 13 flat years

name: Druckenmiller - long D-mark
entry_exit: ~$1bn position Soros told him to double ('You call that a position?'); after the Wall fell (Nov 1989) bet on reunification + Bundesbank tightening
ret_risk: DEM +26% vs USD in 13 months after Oct 1989 (FRED); P&L not documented
signals: Fiscal shock of reunification -> Bundesbank must tighten
failure: Bundesbank accommodation
sources: Schwager (1992) The New Market Wizards; macro_fx_trades.csv

name: Soros & Druckenmiller - sterling
instrument: Short GBP vs DEM (forwards/options), ~$10bn at peak
entry_exit: Built through summer 1992; UK left the ERM 16 Sep 1992
ret_risk: >$1bn (GBP ~1bn) on sterling; downside was only the ~2-3% to the ERM floor plus carry
portfolio: ~+15-20% of Quantum NAV in weeks; UK Treasury cost GBP 3.3bn
signals: Peg far above fundamentals (UK recession, 10% rates) vs. tightening Bundesbank; Schlesinger remarks 15 Sep; finite reserves
sizing: ~1.5x NAV - acceptable only because the peg band capped the loss
failure: Realignment or German rate cut -> small loss; France's franc survived similar attacks

name: SoftBank - Alibaba
entry_exit: $20m in 2000 -> ~$58-75bn at the Sept 2014 IPO
portfolio: Small cheque; offset SoftBank's own >90% share-price collapse in 2000-02
signals: Founder quality; China internet adoption
failure: Most of SoftBank's 2000-era bets failed

name: Amazon from the IPO
entry_exit: Split-adjusted IPO-era price -> 2026
signals: Category-defining platform; founder-led; reinvestment runway
failure: -94% drawdown 1999-2001 and 9.9 years under water (computed)

name: Monster Beverage (Hansen Natural)
signals: Tiny, cheap, then a new product category (energy drinks, 2002)
failure: -96% drawdown 1986-95; 17.6 years under water (computed)

name: Jim Chanos - Enron short
entry_exit: Shorted ~$70-80 after reading the 10-Q; Enron bankrupt Dec 2001 (~$0.26)
ret_risk: ~+100% on the short (max for a short)
signals: Low ROIC, opaque related-party SPEs, heavy insider selling, 'mark-to-market' earnings
failure: Squeeze/borrow recall; many other Kynikos shorts lost for years (funds closed 2023)

name: John Templeton - shorting IPO lock-up expiries
entry_exit: Shorted ~11 days before insider lock-ups expired
signals: Stocks up 3x+ since IPO; mechanical insider supply at lock-up expiry
failure: Mania could keep running; squeeze risk

name: Peter Thiel - Facebook
entry_exit: $500k (2004) -> >$1bn realised after the 2012 IPO
signals: Network effects visible in campus adoption
failure: Venture base rates: most angel bets return zero

name: John Arnold - natural gas vs. Amaranth
entry_exit: Took the other side of Amaranth's winter/summer spreads as they collapsed
portfolio: ~$1bn+ profit; Centaurus reportedly up several hundred % in 2006
signals: Visible crowding: one fund holding a huge share of open interest in a few contract months
failure: Squeeze if Amaranth had been able to hold
sources: MoneyWeek; US Senate PSI (2007) report on Amaranth

name: Cornwall Capital (Ledley, Mai, Hockett)
instrument: Cheap long-dated options; then CDS on AA tranches of subprime CDOs
entry_exit: $110k Schwab account (2003) -> ~$12-30m by 2006 -> ~$80m+ gain on subprime protection (2007)
decisions: Dozens of small bets + 1 big one
signals: Options priced with thin tails on binary situations; AA tranches insured for ~0.5%/yr
sizing: Many small premium bets; premium never large vs. capital
failure: Counterparty (Bear/Lehman) and bleed
sources: Lewis (2010) The Big Short; Cornwall Capital (Wikipedia)

name: John Paulson - subprime CDS
entry_exit: Bought protection from mid-2006 (~1-2%/yr premium); collected 2007-08
signals: Record house-price/income; collapsing lending standards; home-price stalls wipe out BBB tranches; protection cheap
sizing: Dedicated funds; premium modest vs. capital
failure: Bleed while housing kept rising; bank counterparties
sources: Zuckerman (2009) The Greatest Trade Ever; WSJ; Institutional Investor

name: Michael Burry - Scion subprime CDS
entry_exit: Bought from 2005; investor revolt & side-pocket during the 2006 bleed; paid off 2007
signals: Read the prospectuses: teaser-rate ARMs resetting 2007
failure: Nearly lost his investors before being proven right

name: Kyle Bass - Hayman subprime
entry_exit: Started 2005 with $33m
signals: As Paulson
failure: Later 'next big short' bets (JGBs, HKD peg) did not pay; 1.6%/yr 2008-mid-2015

name: Andrew Lahde - subprime
entry_exit: Small fund (~$80m by 2008); closed Oct 2008 citing counterparty risk
signals: As Paulson
failure: Counterparty default (why he quit)

name: David Einhorn - Lehman (and Allied Capital)
entry_exit: Allied: 2002-09 campaign netted only ~$35m; Lehman: short from Jul 2007, public case 2007-08, bankrupt Sep 2008
signals: Leverage, questionable marks, shrinking funding
failure: Years of regulatory/PR war (Allied); squeezes
sources: Einhorn (2008) Fooling Some of the People; Institutional Investor

name: Porsche SE - Volkswagen options
entry_exit: Disclosed 26 Oct 2008 -> VW ord. EUR 211 -> >EUR 1,005 intraday (28 Oct); free float <6% vs. ~12% short interest

signals: Stake-building via undisclosed cash-settled options
failure: Porsche then nearly collapsed under ~EUR 10bn debt and was absorbed by VW (2009)
sources: Harvard Law corpgov (2021) study summary; Porsche disclosure

name: Buffett - Goldman Sachs & Bank of America rescue capital

name: Tesla 2019 -> 2021

name: SNB floor removal - the long-franc convexity side

name: Brexit night (Crispin Odey)
